cards.front: What lets a magnet pull a paper clip across a small gap without touching it?
cards.back: A **field** acts on the clip, which has the right property (it responds to magnetism), so a force is exerted without any contact.
cards.hint: Think about what has to touch what for a force to act.

cards.back: A region in which a **mass** experiences a gravitational force. Every object with mass creates one around itself.

cards.front: Which of the three field types can never repel, and why?
cards.back: **Gravitational** fields, because they act only on mass and gravity is always attractive.
cards.hint: Look at the Force row of the comparison table.

cards.front: What is the gravitational field strength near the Earth's surface, and what is its unit?
cards.back: About $9.8\,\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$. Each kilogram of mass there feels a force of about 9.8 N.
cards.hint: Think of force per kilogram of mass.

cards.front: What is the gravitational force on a 3 kg mass near the Earth's surface?
cards.back: About $29.4\,\text{N}$, since $3 \times 9.8 = 29.4$ using the field strength of about $9.8\,\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$.
cards.hint: Multiply the mass by the field strength.

cards.back: A region where a **charge** experiences an electric force. A charged object creates one around itself.

cards.front: How is the direction of an electric field defined?
cards.back: It is the direction of the force on a **positive** charge placed in the field.
cards.hint: Compare with how the direction of a magnetic field is defined for a north pole.

cards.front: In which direction does the magnetic force on a moving charge act?
cards.back: At **right angles** to both its velocity and the magnetic field. A stationary charge feels no magnetic force.
cards.hint: Consider a charge that is not moving first.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to think field lines are paths that an object must follow?
cards.back: Field lines show the **direction of the force** at each point. They are not routes the object has to travel along.
cards.hint: Think about what the arrow on a line tells you.

cards.front: Why can two field lines never cross each other?
cards.back: At a crossing point the field would have two directions. A field has only **one direction** at each point.
cards.hint: Think about a single point in the field.

cards.front: What does the spacing of field lines tell you about a field?
cards.back: Lines **closer together** show a stronger field; lines further apart show a weaker field.

cards.front: How are field lines drawn in a uniform field?
cards.back: They are **parallel and equally spaced**, because the field has the same strength and direction everywhere.
cards.hint: Think about how the spacing looks across the whole region.

cards.front: Why is a field not a substance that fills space?
cards.back: A field only describes the **force** an object with the right property would feel at each point. It is not material.
cards.hint: Think about what the field is used to measure.
